newsitem.title: UK: EBRD wants more action on E.European corruption.
newsitem.headline: EBRD wants more action on E.European corruption.

text.p: Former Soviet bloc states have made major progress in the transition to market economies but need to do more to root out fraud and corruption, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development said on Monday.

EBRD Chairman Ruairi Quinn said at the opening of the bank's annual meeting in London that the bank would not achieve its objectives unless the components of a modern civic society emerged in the 26 countries in which it operates.

"There has been progress, in spite of slippage, and there have been significant achievements in democratisation, in privatisation and the attraction of both foreign direct and portfolio investment," he said.
EBRD President Jacques de Larosiere listed legal uncertainties, taxation systems and crime and corruption as obstacles facing investors.
"There is corruption, crime and the arbitrary interference of some officials in private sector business activities," he said.
"Although these are far from being the rule, they remain a source of concern and have, in some cases, complicated or even compromised the bank's own operations."
Officials said the bank's comments were intended to make clear to former communist countries that although they have made remarkable progress, they should not become complacent.
Quinn said states had to ensure the rule of law, efficient market regulation and impartial treatment of commercial contracts.
"Corporate governance and micro-regulation must be improved if the reforms are to take root and if domestic savings and further foreign investment are to be attracted," he said.
The EBRD was set up in 1991 to assist the centralised economies of eastern Europe and the former Soviet Union in becoming market democracies.

Economic progress has varied. The Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary have joined the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), grouping richer industrial countries, and are leading candidates to join the European Union.
Some of them even have higher bank credit ratings than EU countries.
The bank is shifting its focus more towards Russia and former Soviet states where reform is at an early stage.
But the need for legal and administrative reform, to combat corruption and boost investor confidence, has become a key theme of the meeting, which continues on Tuesday.
British Overseas Development Minister Lynda Chalker told the meeting investors needed better protection.

"Quick profits will not necessarily be conducive to growth. This does not imply a return to government economic controls, but means establishing regulatory frameworks that protect the saver and investor from unscrupulous businessmen," she said.
The bank has in the past been accused of a lack of financial control and has come under pressure to apply strict banking principles in its lending.

Some of the more advanced economies have called for the bank to become more of a traditional commercial lender. But Quinn said it must not lose sight of its mission to assist in transition and should not be afraid to take risks.
"The importance of the outcome for all of us, the scale of the task being undertaken and the timescale involved all call for risk-taking in furthering the process," he said.

De Larosiere stressed the social aspects of transition, which he acknowledged brought pain and upheaval to ordinary people. "Economic reform must bring, and be seen to bring, material benefits for the people," he said.
